analysis.one_liner: Lets student loan debt be wiped out in bankruptcy like other debts.
analysis.headline: The bill to let student borrowers discharge their loans in bankruptcy was introduced in October 2024 and died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, federal law singles out student loans: even if you file for bankruptcy and lose everything else, you generally cannot erase your student debt unless you can prove the debt causes 'undue hardship' — a standard so strict that most people never even try. This bill would delete that exception, so student loans would be treated like credit card debt, medical bills, or any other unsecured debt: dischargeable in bankruptcy when a person truly cannot pay. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never moved again before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Student borrowers in genuine financial distress — people who lose a job, face illness, or are buried by private loans — would regain the same escape hatch everyone else has for unpayable debt. Roughly 43 million Americans hold student debt, and the fastest-growing slice is older borrowers and people who never finished school. The change would also give lenders a reason to bargain: the threat of real bankruptcy makes restructuring debt cheaper for both sides.

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the bankruptcy code's exception for student loans, so they could be discharged like any other unsecured debt instead of facing the near-impossible 'undue hardship' standard.
The change applies to bankruptcy cases filed on or after the bill's enactment, so it takes effect immediately rather than phasing in.

analysis.who_pays: Lenders and servicers of student loans, especially private lenders, would absorb more losses and likely raise rates or tighten underwriting to price in the risk. Taxpayers would bear some of the cost for federal loans discharged in bankruptcy, since the federal government is the largest holder of student debt. Borrowers who repay could face somewhat higher interest rates than they otherwise would.

drawbacks.text: Discharging federal student debt shifts those losses to taxpayers, who ultimately back the loans — a real cost, though it is what bankruptcy means for any government-guaranteed credit.

Lenders would likely respond by raising interest rates or lending less, since bankruptcy risk makes student loans more expensive to hold; the honest case for the current exception is that it keeps credit cheaper and more available.

Critics of dischargeability argue some borrowers could strategically file for bankruptcy soon after graduation to shed debt they could afford to repay, an abuse the 'undue hardship' rule was designed to prevent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real but one-sided in the current system: the 'undue hardship' standard is so strict that it effectively denies bankruptcy protection to an entire class of debtors, while every other kind of unsecured debt — including gambling debts — can be discharged. The taxpayer cost and possible rate increases are genuine, but they are the same costs society already accepts for credit cards, medical bills, and small business loans. A well-designed version would balance access with abuse prevention; this bill simply equalized treatment, which is a defensible starting point rather than a fully tuned design.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which never took it up; it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Jerrold Nadler introduced the Student Borrower Bankruptcy Relief Act on October 4, 2024, with 19 cosponsors, all Democrats.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced, and no further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no vote.
The bill would have deleted the provision of federal bankruptcy law (11 U.S.C. § 523(a)(8)) that makes student loans nondischargeable except in cases of 'undue hardship'.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan lenders, servicers, and collection agencies keep the single most valuable legal protection in consumer lending: the near-impossibility of erasing student debt in bankruptcy. Borrowers in financial distress gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strike the student loan exception from the bankruptcy code.

for.name: 19 Democratic cosponsors
for.role: Original cosponsors, including Reps. Correa, Tlaib, Jayapal, Waters, and Raskin
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors on the day of introduction; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Jim Jordan (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on October 4, 2024 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and a Republican-run committee never advanced it.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and collection agencies
industries.note: The bill would end their guaranteed ability to pursue borrowers through old age, illness, or insolvency, since discharged debt could no longer be chased. Their revenue depends on the nondischargeability rule the bill deletes.

Private education loans would become risky like other unsecured consumer credit, likely forcing higher rates or tighter lending. The current rule gives these lenders collateral-like protection on loans backed by nothing but a signature.

Discharging federal loans in bankruptcy would shift some losses onto taxpayers, but it would also end a system where the government collects with powers unavailable to any other creditor — wage garnishment without a court order, and liens — from borrowers who genuinely cannot pay.
